what: A32 frontier pilot: instrumented joint structure branch-and-bound over PARTIAL contact structures, s0 = 3.8771
findings: ENGINE VALIDATED against A31 at every k it reaches.  With the per-wall cap switched off the A32 branch-and-bound reproduces A31's MAIN counts and all three branch counts EXACTLY (k=3: 10/9/1/24, k=4: 140/121/4/194, k=5: 2275/1989/18/1979, k=6: 41951/37022/109/25890).  With the certified per-wall cap 3 promoted to a hard prune (as the A32 brief directs) it reproduces A31's wallcap3 columns exactly at k=3..7 (10, 131, 2007, 33967, 623194) and the non-thin sub-counts (1, 17, 245, 4001, 67130).

THE DECISIVE STRUCTURAL FACT: in a branch-and-bound whose kills are all MONOTONE, every surviving complete structure is a leaf that must be visited, so the node count is bounded BELOW by the leaf count.  Measured overhead (partial nodes visited / MAIN leaves) is 80, 73, 73, 86, 122 at k = 3..7 -- it GROWS, roughly linearly in k.  Early kill therefore cannot beat A31's flat survivor count; it can only avoid materialising what A31 filtered out.

EARLY-KILL COLLAPSE FACTOR vs A31's flat counts at k=7.  A32 visits 76,071,280 partial nodes to produce the same 623,194 leaves.  A31 actually evaluated 4,198,469,470 (A-rep, wall-mask) rows for the same level, so early kill collapses the WORK by 55x; against A31's unfiltered orbit count R0 = 14,828,211,568 the factor is 195x, and against its own cheaply-filtered row R5 = 207,791,913 only 2.7x.  The collapse is real but modest, and it is bought at 175x the per-object cost.

AND IT DOES NOT PAY FOR ITSELF.  A32's k=7 tree cost 1736 s on 6 workers (22.8 us per partial node, pure Python) against A31's 557 s for the vectorised flat enumeration of the same k=7 level.  Node-at-a-time branch-and-bound is 3x SLOWER in wall clock despite visiting 55x fewer objects: 137 us of CORE time per partial node (about 64% of it the canonical form, ~50 us the cascade itself) swamps the pruning gain.  A bitset/C implementation plus a nauty-style canonical labelling would need roughly a 50x per-node speed-up merely to draw level with vectorised flat enumeration.

FRONTIER GROWTH.  Partial nodes per target core size: 798, 9502, 145702, 2,934,176, 76,071,280 for k = 3..7; successive ratios 11.9, 15.3, 20.1, 25.9 -- LINEAR in k, i.e. factorial-times-exponential growth, exactly the shape A31 found for the flat counts.  Extrapolated to k = 11: 5.6e12 (log-linear fit) to 1.4e14 (ratio-linear fit) partial nodes at the GRAPH level alone, i.e. 2e5 - 5e6 CPU-hours at the measured 137 us of core time per partial node.

MODE D (decorations branched jointly with the structure).  Tilt propagation reproduces A31's exact Level-1 counts on every graph tested (21/21 exact agreements), so the decorated engine is validated too.  Per-edge decoration survival factor (geometric mean over sampled MAIN graphs, full cascade tilt+rotation+L2): 2.93, 4.18, 3.87, 5.14, 5.49 at k = 3..7, against A31's tilt-only 3.00, 3.79, 4.59, 5.34, 5.85.  The two new monotone decoration filters therefore buy about 6% per edge at k=7 -- a factor ~4 over the ~23 edges of a k=11 core.  Projected decorated fan-out per graph at k=11: 1e19 - 1e20, against A31's tilt-only 6.5e18.  NO change of order of magnitude.  Pooled per-child kill rates on the sampled tree at k=7: tilt 12.9%, rotation system 4.2% of what tilt leaves (and rising fast with k: 0.0, 0.6, 1.0, 2.0, 4.2%), L2 struts 3.5% of the rest.

L2 COLLINEARITY IS THE ONE REAL WIN, AND IT IS SMALLER THAN HOPED.  The brief expected the codimension-1 strut equation to make the thin branch die fast.  It does kill whole graphs: with an EXACT capped depth-first search over the decoration tree, 4/10 MAIN graphs at k=3 and 9/25 at k=4 are PROVEN to have no surviving decoration at all, and every one of them is a thin (degree-2) graph -- about 43% of thin graphs, 0% of non-thin.  That is a factor ~1.6 on the graph count, not the ~10x that promoting L2 to a hard prune would give (A31 gap G5).  The remaining thin graphs survive because their degree-2 squares carry at least one contact whose force direction is set by the NEIGHBOUR's tilt, which the slot-level test cannot decide (deferred; logged).

ABLATION (k=6, closed frontier 51,690 with the full cascade): metric interval feasibility is by far the strongest monotone stage (off -> 311,622, x6.0), then the L1 EXTENSIBILITY prune X1 (off -> 103,064, x2.0 -- and it is free, it is the only stage that turns a non-monotone structural requirement into an early kill), then planarity (x1.6) and the per-wall cap 3 (x1.3).  The Euler bound and the Euler budget never fire at k <= 6.

THE STRENGTHENED METRIC TEST ADDS NOTHING.  Closing the interval distance system under the triangle inequality (Floyd on the upper bounds, reverse triangle on the lower bounds) is EXACTLY as strong as A31's L5(a) broad phase at k <= 6: disabling either one alone leaves the frontier unchanged (3601 at k=5, both directions), and disabling both gives 19,187.  The wall-box + hop-distance system is already triangle-closed.

STAGES 4-6 (Farkas / case-LP / Fritz John) FIRE ZERO TIMES ON STRUCTURE-DERIVED CELLS.  On 30 sampled nodes across k = 4,5,6 the Gordan/Farkas first-order test found no improving direction (0/30), interval SAT never certified infeasibility (0/30), no pair menu was ever empty, the case-LP stub was feasible on 10/10, and the cheap FJ range exclusion excluded 0/10.  Cost 0.11-0.31 s per node -- 5,000-13,000x the cost of the combinatorial cascade for zero kills.  Pinning every tilt to the zero class (the strongest decoration information available) cuts the active row set from ~510 to ~190 but still yields no kill.  This confirms A30's verdict from the other side: the first-order tests need cells of half-width ~1e-4, and a structure-derived cell is ~1.4 wide.

STAGE-6 STRUCTURAL NOTE.  A contact structure fixes which CONTACTS are active but not which SELECTION ROWS are; on a wide cell the active-row menu has ~500-750 members instead of the ~35 a square FJ system needs.  A Krawczyk FJ solve is therefore not even well-posed at a structure node until the decoration is committed -- the FJ solve belongs strictly below the decoration layer, not at the structure layer.

GO/NO-GO: NO-GO, decisively.  The k=11 frontier of the joint structure-and-decoration branch-and-bound projects to 5.6e12 - 1.4e14 nodes at the graph level and ~1e30 decorated leaves -- 7 to 24 orders of magnitude above the 1e4-1e6 solvable-node target, and the growth is factorial-times-exponential, not exponential.  Early kill buys a factor ~200 against naive enumeration and LOSES to vectorised flat enumeration on wall clock.  The structure-first campaign cannot be rescued by better search over this node space; it needs a lemma that collapses the space itself (promoting L2 or the Maxwell row count to hard prunes, or a wall-to-wall chain argument that fixes the core to O(1) shapes).

SOUNDNESS CANARY: PASS.  Trump's structure (11 loaded squares, 14 square-square + 11 square-wall contacts, s = 3.8770835900228) survives all 110 mode-G prefixes of an 11-step vertex insertion, closes as MAIN (L1/L3/L6/L7 all true, not thin), and its REAL decoration read off the certificate (7 flush + 7 corner-on-edge square-square contacts, gauge residual 4e-16) survives all 25 mode-D prefixes of tilt propagation, the rotation-system test and the L2 strut test.

gaps.text: The brief lists 'flush-mandatory' among the structural requirements to be applied as an extensibility check.  The Soundness ledger of structure_lemmas.md marks the Maxwell row count m >= 3k+1 (which is what makes flush mandatory) SOFT, and the brief itself says the ledger governs.  Resolved in favour of the ledger: flush-mandatory is NOT used as a kill anywhere in A32.  If it were ever proved, A31's G7 says it would be a very strong filter.

'Add a square' is realised as the OUTER loop over the target core size K (one tree per K, exactly as A31 counts one level per k), not as a branch move inside a single tree.  Consequence: the X1 extensibility prune is sharp (a square's deficiency can only be met by the K-k squares not yet introduced), which is why the frontier is finite at all; a single tree over all K <= 11 would have a much weaker X1 and a much larger frontier.

Edge-at-a-time branching is done WITHIN a vertex step (the new square's k+4 slots are decided one at a time with the cascade on every prefix), not globally over an undecided edge set.  A fully edge-at-a-time tree with 'undecided' semantics would be much larger still: with all pairs undecided, the sparse junk structures that X1 kills here survive every monotone test.

Mode D is measured per graph with Knuth's random-path estimator (unbiased, 150 walks per graph, 10 graphs per k) except where an exact capped DFS was run.  The estimator has heavy tails: the reported stderr columns are large for the biggest graphs.

The L2 dead-graph scan is exact only where the capped DFS was exhausted: 10/10 graphs at k=3, 18/25 at k=4 (cap 120k child evaluations), and 6/15 at k=5 with the cap raised to 1.5M.  k=6 was abandoned after one graph -- at cap 1.5M no k=6 tree is exhausted.  The dead FRACTION at k >= 5 is therefore a lower bound (3/15 measured) and the clean numbers are k=3 and k=4.

The L2 test is applied at the slot level only.  The cases it defers (a degree-2 square with a contact whose normal is set by the neighbour's tilt) need the metric line-of-action condition, which is a genuine codimension-1 equation that interval arithmetic on structure-derived boxes cannot see.  Closing those cases is the single most valuable follow-up, and would push the thin-branch kill from ~43% of thin graphs toward A31's 90%.

The rotation-system test is applied to the square-square subgraph only (A31's G9): the rotation at a wall node is not determined by a decoration.  Wall slots do influence the ordering around each square, but the wall nodes' own rotations, and consistency with the L4 drawing, are not enforced.

k = 8 was not run.  The canonical form is a minimum over S_k x D4 evaluated as |G| vector adds; at k=8 the group has 322,560 elements (8x k=7) and the projected level cost is ~12 core-hours plus 155 MB of group tables per worker.  A real campaign needs a nauty-style canonical labelling, not a group sweep.

Everything at k > 7 is extrapolation from k = 3..7, not a bound.  The two models (log-linear in k, and linear-in-k successive ratios) differ by a factor 25 at k = 11, and the ratio model is the better fit to the measured ratios, so 1.4e14 is the more honest number.

Like A31, the count is PER CORE: the 11-k rattlers are not placed, and the lambda0 = 0 and L3 self-stress branches are counted separately (k=7: 233,057 and 843) and are not part of MAIN.  Each still needs its own excludable row system.

RAM is guarded structurally, not by measurement: the search is depth-first inside each vertex step (stack depth <= k+4) and only one level's canonical mask list is held in memory (int per node; the largest, k=7 level 7, is 857,094 ints), plus a --node-cap abort.  psutil is not installed in this environment so no live RSS probe was added; peak observed working set was ~330 MB per worker at k=7, dominated by the 40,320 x 49 group-action table.

X2, the Euler-budget extensibility prune, was first written as |E| + sum_i deficiency_i <= 3K+2, which over-prunes because one future edge can retire deficiency at BOTH of its endpoints; it was corrected to |E| + ceil(sum/2).  X2 fires ZERO times at every k measured (both the ablation and the kill-share table show 0) and the k=3..7 leaf counts are identical before and after the correction and match A31 exactly, so no reported number is affected.  Recorded because the same trap will reappear in any extensibility prune that counts edge endpoints.

sec/node is measured with 6 Python worker processes on a 20-core machine and includes the canonical-form computation, which is about 64% of the core time at k=7 (7.4M canonical forms at 0.9 ms each).  The cascade itself is ~50 us of core time per node.
